subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
That this House regrets that the Prime Minister has once again broken an election campaign promise, this time by failing to maintain quotas on imports of shoes and by compounding this betrayal by failing to make adequate provision for the thousands of workers whose jobs are adversely affected.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to put this very important issue before the House of Commons, today on Monday, November 25, 1985, a few days after hearing an announcement that has practically lifted all quotas from shoe imports.
As the motion indicates, the Prime Minister went to the Eastern Townships in May 1984. We must understand that textiles, clothing and footwear are extremely important industries that are very job intensive and absolutely essential to the economy of the Eastern Townships.
Last week, when the decision was known, certain people close to the Prime Minister claimed that Mr. Mulroney had never made a commitment and that the Prime Minister had never promised he would maintain or extend the quotas. Therefore, with your leave, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to a document which I find very significant, very interesting and very revealing, concerning the announcement or commitment made by the Prime Minister at the time. I am going to quote from a newspaper article reporting on that commitment, and it says: "A Conservative Government would not lift import quotas set by this country with respect to footwear, textiles and clothing". The quota policy would remain as such, said Mr. Mulroney, who stated he was not in favour of free trade in these particular sectors. He added that he would not alter his position, despite possible pressures from Common Market countries and the United States to reduce quotas on footwear and textile products imported into Canada. He added: I will certainly say so to President Reagan when I meet him in Washington next month. I will see to it that our interests are protected at all times. Friendships like ours are worth something, he said. Neighbours like us are worth a lot, maintained the Conservative Leader.
Mr. Speaker, today, although there might be a case for saying that Mr. Mulroney, the Prime Minister, did not make a firm commitment specifically concerning the footwear industry and did not make a firm commitment on the issue of extending quotas, if we put his commitments and his statements in their proper context, bearing in mind that the footwear industry is a very important sector in the Eastern Townships, I do not think there can be any ambiguity or confusion: this was indeed a very formal commitment.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as indicated in the motion, we are still faced with a very serious situation where this Government has literally betrayed the trust it received from Canadian men and women on September 4, and it has done so in an area where the consequences will indeed be disastrous.
According to the most optimistic figures given last week by the Manufacturers' Association, in the very near future only about 4,000 out of 20,000 jobs in the footwear industry will be left. What is extremely discouraging and disheartening, along with the catastrophic reduction in the number of jobs in the footwear industry, is the fact that in a great many cases, these industries cannot expect to obtain any kind of substitution or solution or remedy, since most are located in areas away from the large urban centres, areas where it is extremely difficult and problematic to interest investors in investing in replacement industries, to make up for the jobs lost in the footwear sector.
Mr. Speaker, this forecast for the footwear industry seems much closer to reality than what the Government appears to be saying. We must understand that the previous Government set these quotas, which were renewed for three years at a time, and when this Government came to power, the quotas were to continue until the end of May, 1986. One of this Government's first decisions was to shorten very significantly the deadline for the quotas by making them end on November 30 of this year, which is this week.
The study used by the Government in making its decision, the anti-dumping report, was released last June. Therefore the antidumping report conclusions were known as early as last June. So why did the Government wait until the penultimate week of November to make its position public? Respectfully, Mr. Speaker, we maintain that its mind was set, that the decision had long since been made, but it waited until the last minute in the hope that consumers, workers and the industry

would not raise too much of a fuss about this totally catastrophic conclusion.
Government Members have two explanations to justify their decision. First they tell us that the most sweeping and comprehensive study in this Field does recommend the outright abolition of quotas. That is their main argument, their first excuse to do away with quotas. Then they go on to maintain that, over the last eight years, Canadians have paid the astronomical amount of $400 million to $500 million more than it would have cost them had quotas not been in force.
In my estimation, Mr. Speaker, both arguments can easily be demolished in either case. First, concerning the antidumping report, the reader will be amazed at the findings if only he goes to the trouble of reading it very carefully page after page. I would even say that its conclusion flies in the face of logic with respect to the main thrust of the report. The best way to substantiate my views on the famous antidumping report is to quote parts of it.
This can be found on page 132: "If unrestricted and quota imports are added up, it becomes obvious that over-all imports soared by 10 million pairs since 1980, an increase of 23 per cent." One has to admit that imports rose considerably between 1980 and 1984 when they were subject to quotas. It being so, how can anybody conclude that imports will not go up if they are not restricted? To me that is a rather illogical statement.
Here is another passage of the antidumping report, from page 49 this time: "Since direct imports enable retailers to avoid paying the importer's margin, in all likelihood they would boost both their volume and share of imports if there were no quotas." Here again it does not quite jibe with the Government position.
A further quotation: "Net Government receipts would be higher after the removal of quotas, mainly as a result of more tariff levies due to rising imports."
One last extract from page 62 of the famous antidumping report goes like this: "It can be expected that quota removal- immediate, total, partial or gradual-will spur imports, and manufacturers might well decide to become importers since the different economic climate would pave the way for a new market approach".
Mr. Speaker, I could go on like this for half an hour or three quarters of an hour, quoting and repeating statements and findings which abound in the antidumping report, finally to conclude that they openly contradict the logical arguments from which they are derived. It seems to me this would have been a good reason for the Government to reject this study, for indeed it would not have been the first time a Government had turned down a study however complete and exhaustive it might have been. The interest of workers and their jobs was the issue,
but the Government is hiding behind what is clearly an unacceptable report.
They do not hesitate to pick out only those parts of the report which seem to strengthen their case, going as far as to stress the second argument to the effect that consumers have shelled out $400 million to $500 million simply because of the quotas.
The anti-dumping report-and I think that the government should be honest enough to recognize it-mentions that this assessment is not at all scientific and is based solely on studies which have every chance not to be valid, and that it is an affirmation based on an approximation. On the one hand, there is nothing final, specific or especially scientific about this assessment.
On the other hand, let me tell you that according to a study or analysis made by an organization representing thousands of people in order to refute this argument, there will be some $3 billion in social cost over the next eight years following the Government's announcement. Canadian men and women will pay as much as $3 billion in unemployment insurance and welfare benefits over the next eight years following the measure which was announced last week and which will result in the very short run in a loss of several thousand jobs.
Mr. Speaker, there is another reason, as basic as the first for which I feel that the decision announced last week will not benefit consumers or serve their best interest.
One need only visit shopping centres to realize that almost everywhere people use Canadian products, Canadian footwear as points of reference.
1 am sure that my hon. colleagues opposite have had that experience too: a pair of Canadian shoes is offered at a price of, say, $79.95. Right beside it is a pair of imported shoes with a price of $69.95. Consumers are therefore attracted by the imported product which is $10 cheaper than the Canadian product. I suggest that people who are not well informed will not see much difference between these two products. The Canadian man or woman who chooses the imported pair of shoes will feel he or she has saved $10.
However, what one should know, Mr. Speaker, is that the retailer who is asking $80 for the Canadian product paid approximately $40 for it. On the other hand, he is asking $69 for the imported product for which he has paid $15 or $16. The retailer, therefore, will do everything to try and convince consumers to choose imported goods.
Mr. Speaker, you certainly realize that, so far, the Canadian consumer in my example is clearly ahead, for he has saved $10. But what about the respecting quality of the two pairs of shoes? I suggest that the Canadian product is of much better quality than the imported product. I also feel that getting rid of this point of reference would be extremely dangerous, for as
November 25, 1985

soon as retailers will no longer use Canadian products for comparison, consumers will have to pay the price, and a very high one at that.
There is another angle to this situation. I would ask my Hon. colleagues of the fair sex to visit chain stores and to go shopping for a pair of women shoes. You will find out it is extremely difficult, extremely painful. Salespeople will even tell you that Canadian products have no style, that they do not keep up with the latest fashion. They will invoke all kinds of arguments that are simply not relevant. Only someone who does not know anything about that field could make such statements. The products we make here in Canada are equal or superior in quality to what the import market has to offer, and there is only one reason we cannot find Canadian women's shoes in the stores. It is purely and simply because the retailer does not get a mark-up comparable to the one he gets on imported shoes. It is due exclusively to the fact that on shoes made in Canada, his mark-up or profit margin is only 50 per cent while it is much lower on imported shoes.
On the other hand, we must also understand that this is a very special sector where retailing is virtually under the control of a few big companies. Independent retailers, even though they number more than 4,000 in Canada, did not have a say in that matter nor any chance of expressing their opinions and even at that level, the decision the Government announced last week will prove disastrous. We will see small independent retailers close their business in the next few months and weeks. They will be replaced by the big chains that import and control the retail market, and believe me, their main objective is not the interest of the consumers, but their own profit, first and foremost the improvement of their businesses' viability, at the expense of the ordinary consumer.
So, Mr. Speaker, this is a disastrous decision. On the other hand the only alternative indicated in the Minister's statement where three aspects of an already existing program are mentioned in a solution which is already available to my riding. I come from an asbestos-producing areas and in view of the difficult times experienced by the asbestos two or three years ago, we became a designated area which is to all practical purposes what the Minister is now offering the workers in the shoe industry. In conclusion I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that those measures have not changed the situation a iota nor resulted in any permanent job creation because the problem is due to an economic slowdown in the asbestos sector. Now this is the alternative which is being offered to the Canadian industry shoe workers.
Mr. Speaker, as we shall learn about the closing of one or more plants in the months ahead, I hope that the Government, in all fairness will reverse its decision, and will come up with one based on the interests not of the importers but of the

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully while the Hon. Member was speaking about this issue, and 1 believe that if he is so deeply concerned, it is because of the geographic location of his constituency. In his motion, he mentions an election campaign promise. I would like him to tell me what promise or what commitment the Liberal Party made regarding footwear import quotas during the campaign and where 1 can find it because, when I was preparing my intervention for today this week-end, I tried to find the commitment of the Liberal Party as concerns footwear quotas and I found nothing. I was trying to explain . . . May I continue with my question? I was trying to explain why, very often, Governments have a tendency to do such a thing as referring the issue to a tribunal when a difficult decision has to be made, and I would like to point out in passing that newspaper reports are generally quite favourable to this decision because the medias believe that it shows courage. We then have to ask this question: What was the commitment of the Liberal Party as regards footwear quotas during the last election campaign? I would like to know.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
I would like to thank the Hon. Member opposite for his interesting question. I shall simply tell him that the quotas were established, maintained and reinstated under the Liberal Government on the one hand. On the other, and I invite the Hon. Member to listen carefully to what I will tell him, when the quotas were about to be lifted the last time, the Government was under the same pressures as you were. The difference was, Mr. Speaker, that this political party, and I am speaking of course about the Liberal Party, included men and women who had the courage to protest strongly against the decision made by Cabinet at the time and to say: "If you put this forward, we shall not support it." This is easy to verify: it is on the public record. If you are in the least interested in this issue, you can check these facts by simply asking for the documents. You will then see that the Government reversed its decision and re-established the quotas for the industry. Moreover, I would like to remind you that there had been a demonstration on Parliament Hill involving 5,500 workers from Ontario and Quebec, as well as four Liberal Members of Parliament, even though their party was in power at the time. The demonstrations included myself and three of my colleagues, and even some of your own colleagues. Some of your colleagues were even saying at the time: "If the country had a Progressive Conservative Government, you would have not only quotas, but also a clear and precise policy. There would not be such loopholes as now exist under your Government."

1 recognize that the previous Government established quotas. I recognize that these quotas were not perfect and that the situation was not what it should have been because of certain loopholes. As for you, you are getting rid of the quotas, and as for the few that remain their effectiveness is still limited by an obvious loophole, as big as the House of Commons. Here is a very simple example of what I mean: You say that girls' and women's footwear are subject to quotas. What about unisex footwear? Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would like to invite those of you who are concerned about the shoe industry to do what we did ourselves and to oppose your Government if you want to protect the jobs in this industry.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question on the same subject. We made, I believe, three main mistakes in the Canadian strategy regarding the shoe industry.
The first one was the removal, by the Liberal Government, of quotas on leather shoes between November 30, 1981 and July 9, 1982. Imports increased dramatically during that period.
The second, Mr. Speaker, mentioned in the report itself, is that before 1981 there was no restructuring in that industry. That is what the report says. It means that after four years of quotas, there has been no change whatsoever. Modernization, which should be at the centre of any effective strategy in this industry, did not take place.
The third mistake-and this is also mentioned in the report, I believe-is that the quota system set up after 1982 was too weak. We find that in the report. As a consequence, had a high level of imports despite the quotas. Given all these mistakes and difficulties, is it possible for a Liberal Member to say that it is a Conservative rather than a Liberal problem?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
This is a good question, Mr. Speaker, as it gives me the opportunity to make a short comment. New Democrats can say whatever they want because they will never be more than fifteen or twenty. But the answer to the question of the Hon. Member is yes.
Shoe manufacturers, Mr. Speaker, want 50 per cent of consumption. However, statistics show that they have, at this very moment, only 40 per cent, and the Government wants to reduce their share to 9 to 12 per cent. This is what is offered to the manufacturers. Under the Liberal Government they had between 48 and 40 per cent of consumption. It is a whole lot more than what is being offered to them now. Nobody is perfect. Personally, I would have preferred a 50 per cent share for a period of five years. Nevertheless, they had 40 per cent and they are now given only 10 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision to abolish quotas in the shoe industry made by the Minister last Wednesday is a perfect symbol of everything which is wrong with the present Government. On the one hand, it reveals the insincerity of the Government in terms of promises which were made during the election campaign and, on the other hand, it reveals its insensitivity to Canada's working families. Finally, and perhaps ultimately most significantly, it reveals the incompetence of the Government when it comes to important economic decisions. I would like to comment on all three of these matters.

Mr. Speaker, this Government is not taking its promises seriously. On the contrary it makes no bones about breaking them. In Sherbrooke, last year, Mr. Mulroney, then Leader of the Opposition, had promised that a Tory Government would maintain quotas on footwear imports, that he would not give in despite pressures from the EEC and the United States. Mr. Mulroney had then understood that a committee set up by the Liberals could suggest the removal of quotas, but in spite of the promises made in Sherbrooke, in spite of a promise as a new Government, the Prime Minister is implementing the recommendations of the Liberal committee. In reaching such a decision, he has deceived Canadians, he has betrayed the workers in the Canadian footwear industry.

In sector after sector, promises made in a particular part of Canada to a particular group of Canadian workers during the election campaign, are now being broken. The most relevant and recent example is, of course, what we are debating here today, the promise made to men and women working in the shoe industry and related industries that quotas would be maintained. This promise, it appears, was rather cynically given before the election and cynically ignored afterwards.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that my Party takes election promises seriously.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
I see the snickering Tory to the left- physically in the House, of course-because his Party obviously does not take its promises seriously. I say to the Tories opposite, because they often like to accuse us of being big spenders, that I am proud to say that the New Democratic Party in 1984, in terms of the costs of its programs which were published before the election, probably came in at the lowest cost of all three Parties. We took care in what we had to say and I just wish that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) had taken care in what he had to say in 1984 and had carried it out in 1985.
I do not want to dwell on that particular point, but it is something I take very seriously indeed. If we are going to encourage constructive thinking about politics, if we are going to have serious debates on the future of our nation, politicians have an obligation to mean what they say, to say what they
November 25, 1985

mean, and if they are elected, to carry out what they promise the people of Canada.
1 would like to turn to another aspect of this question of the performance of the Government which is revealed in this latest decision.

Such a decision shows insensitivity towards laid-off workers. According to the Shoe Manufacturers' Association of Canada and unions operating in that sector, the removal of quotas on shoes will result in the closure of many factories and ultimately in massive lay-offs. Mention has been made of the loss of some 10,000 jobs, 8,000 of which would be in Quebec and probably 5,000 or so in the Montreal area.
In addition to jobs directly related to the manufacture of footwear, the same percentage of jobs, that is 50 per cent, are also threatened in the related industries of tanning and supplies. The manpower in that sector recognized for its great stability is very concerned. Having worked during their lifetime in that sector, workers are worried because they may find it very difficult to find other jobs. They are right.
We should consider also the effects on the communities. For twenty years or so, the factories producing footwear and soles have left cities to relocate in smaller towns in Quebec as well as in other provinces. If those factories have to close, increased unemployment in those communities will reduce the purchasing power of residents which will directly affect the economy of those communities.
In short, we are forsaking that industry, those towns and those workers.
The report contains a little noted comment which I want to stress today. The Minister has not alluded to this very much since he made his decision. The report says: "The upheavals caused will certainly be significant for the industry and the workers affected". The people who made this report were well aware of the consequences for the men and women in the industry.
The decision is not only insensitive to workers in the communities affected, it is also economically foolish. The simplicity and insensitivity of the Government, I regret to say, is equal only to the simplicity and insensitivity of the commentators who have discussed the Government's decision. A frequently stated, sometimes unstated, assumption about the economic process we are now going through-and it directly pertains to this particular decision-is that the Government of Canada must come down, on the one hand, for completely free trade and, on the other, for some kind of permanent quota system. There seem to be, in this Government's mind as in that of previous Governments, Liberal and Conservative alike, only two industrial options. There is the passive industrial option which sees the future of Canada hiding behind high tariff barriers. That, more or less, has been tried in this country in
Supply
the past. The other passive industrial option that this Government seems to be aiming towards is the removal of all barriers, to throw open our country to the winds, to use a delightful euphemism, which prevail in the world economy. I want to stress that both those options are essentially passive in nature. However, in my judgment, no nation in history has come to a position of significant economic prowess by following either of those options, not in the ancient world nor in the modern world. I say to the Minister that these two options are not the only ones open to Canada. There is a third option.
The Government of Canada can play an active, constructive, and imaginative role on a sector by sector basis with the private sector. Together they can work out a strategy for this country in its approach to the world economy which rejects the dual forms of passivity involved in hiding behind a protective mechanism for an indefinite period of time, or throwing caution to the winds and throwing open the doors to the forces of the world economy.
This decision illustrates the Government's tendency to head towards free trade, not having thought out the consequences. The Minister is right when he says, as he does, that the quotas have not really worked. We have had them in place for eight years and the Government's view is that if the quotas were going to work, they ought to have worked by now. Some facts are very pertinent to this argument. First of all, as the Minister knows, some $17 million was allocated under CIRB to this industry. He also knows that during the quota period a very small percentage of the money allocated for modernization has actually been used. In fact, if I remember correctly, only $2.2 million has been used. Therefore, the point is that the modernization process has just begun. Only a small percentage of the money has been used in the way it was intended to be used. However, what does the Government do when it is faced with this reality? It throws up its hands and says, "We have tried, it has not worked, so we will just stop the whole thing and throw the economy-that is these workers we are talking about, men and women and their families as well as their communities, I remind the Minister-to the whims of the market." This is a classic example of what the Liberals have done historically in this country.

You started it, I agree. I say to my Liberal colleagues on my right that I want them to join in the debate. I know they moved the motion. I want them to talk about the issues. The reason I say that we have a typical Liberal solution here is that the Liberals historically threw money at a problem for a number of years and then, if it did not resolve the problem, they went on and did something else instead of trying to make it work. The key point I want to make is that instead of abandoning the program when we know a majority of the firms have just started to carry out the required moderniza-

November 25, 1985

tion, we should be encouraging the completion of this process. The Minister knows and the report shows that these firms are now spending the money allocated for modernization. If we do not encourage the completion of this process, we will just be wasting the money which has been spent so far. Beyond that, most significantly, we will be wasting the lives of the men and women who are going to be losing their jobs. We do not think that makes economic or social sense.
1 cannot put too much emphasis on this point. We had in place a good model of industrial planning which ought to be applied to other sectors. I agree that the firms involved did not respond quickly enough over the past eight years. But, by God, we had begun to see a different approach in other industrial countries-Japan sure as hell, to put it bluntly, would not have thrown its workers out on the street. It would not have just abandoned money like this. We had a good process. The industry was slow in responding but it is doing so now and we should be completing the process to keep those jobs and make this industry competitive in the modern world. The option is really not the kind that the Minister and the Government want to give us. In the near future we want to have quotas in this industry abolished. We want to have the industrial modernization process which was started with this program carried through. Instead of doing that, the Minister is simply abandoning a good idea. In the traditional Liberal way he has thrown some money at it and when that did not produce results in the short run he has stopped it entirely. That is not good planning at all.
I will give one other example of the incompetence that is illustrated by this decision. I regret to say that it is my view that the decision of the Minister and the Government on this issue was shaped simply because of a failure to believe in industrial planning in a mixed economy which plays an important role. The other key factor was the process that is under way for negotiations with the United States on free trade. We are doing all the wrong things. One day we give up Canadian content in the automotive sector, losing Canadian jobs in the process because it does not seem to be compatible with the American model of a comprehensive free trade agreement. Another day we sacrifice Canadian shoeworkers on the altar of the wonderful free trade market. All of this fits into the American strategy but does not fit at all into the Canadian strategy.
While we are busy sacrificing sectors of Canadian workers, significant American figures are talking about getting a resolution of certain bilateral issues such as the importation of logs, pork, and so on. Before the talks commence in a serious way they would like to get the issues resolved. The Conservative Government is busy giving up the interests of Canadian workers in advance. All I can say is that this is no way to conduct major negotiations which go to the heart of the future of the country.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that the decision taken last Wednesday was bad in both the short run and the long run
for Canadian workers in the shoe industry. It was bad for what it says about the Government's view of industrial planning and bad in terms of revealing its attitude toward negotiations with the United States.

Mr. Speaker, of course I have concern for the consumers. If the Member reads the report, as he has perhaps already done, he will notice that the report itself says that the Canadian producers did not increase their prices during the period of the quotas. Therefore, there certainly was not an increase in prices paid, which had a negotiative effect on consumers during this period.
It seems very clear to us in the New Democratic Party that in approaching the economy of Canada one has to look at it in terms of broad concerns, consumer concerns, worker concerns, employment concerns and community concerns. When we address that issue we are prepared to say that there may be some costs to a consumer in any part of Canada to maintain industry in the country. There are only one or two raw materials that we could not get cheaper elsewhere in the world. However, we made a decision a long time ago that a country is about creating opportunity for men and women to work and that is our priority.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I have listened to the debate on footwear over the past few days in this House two things have struck me: The opportunism of the Opposition, an opportunism extending to cynicism, and the lack of sensitivity of the Opposition. It is out of touch with Canadian consumers and Canadian life. Of course, that is nothing new. The other day the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) accused the Government of practising "abstract economic theology". The Government practices nothing of the kind. We deal in economic realities.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: That is a euphemism for selling out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
In this case we are dealing with a 223-page report by the Canadian Import Tribunal which heard 72 witnesses and received 39 written submissions. After the report came out we consulted on its findings with all parties concerned. Abstract economic theory is not our bag. That is what the previous Government practised from its oracle on "Mount Saint Elsewhere". What was the NEP but abstract theory? What was FIRA?
Of course, theory is not involved in the attacks that my hon. friends in the Opposition have been making on the Government's footwear policy. Here they have been forced to resort to smoke and mirrors and to plain political opportunism. Take the charge made by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has broken an election promise made on May 4, 1984. Let us look at the facts.
On May 4 of last year the Liberals were in the middle of their leadership campaign. On May 4 elections were nowhere in sight.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: To continue the chronology, it was not until several weeks later, on June 14 of 1984, that the former Government called on the Canadian Import Tribunal to examine the state of the footwear industry and report its findings within one year. It was not until July 9 that the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, having just been sworn in as Prime Minister of Canada, dissolved Parliament-which he could not sit in anyway-and called the election that put the Government in office with the largest majority in the history of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Now we skip nearly a year. On June 14 of this year the Canadian Import Tribunal, having conducted the most thorough study of the footwear industry ever carried out by any inquiring body, handed down its report. After a full year of study it found that most of the footwear industry no longer needed the protection of import quotas. Indeed, it could no longer benefit from quotas.
Had the tribunal found that import quotas were still desirable, I can assure you that the Government would have
Supply
followed its recommendations and left them in force. That, incidentally, is more than what the previous Government did. In an earlier inquiry into footwear, the tribunal ruled in February, 1981, that the removal of quotas would be harmful to the Canadian footwear industry. Despite this finding, the then Government, in its wisdom, took the quotas off and then had to restore them in a few months. This was the Government that now sits as the Opposition, for very good reason, and whose international trade critic stood up the other day to accuse us-in his entirely unparliamentary word, as recorded on page 8637 of Hansard-of "treason".
By now Canadians are aware that what we have done on footwear is to put into force the recommendations of the Canadian Import Tribunal, a tribunal established and appointed by the previous Government. I would point out that its studies of the footwear industry were exhaustive and that its recommendations were specific and clear. Under the circumstances, I find it extremely difficult to understand how the Liberal Party can adopt a position of opposition on this measure. I suspect some of its own Members may be as confused by its stance as I am.
In light of the fact that the tribunal found that four of the five categories of footwear producers are now able to stand up to foreign competition, is it the Liberal Party's position that we should ignore the tribunal's recommendations and continue quotas that have cost the consumers of Canada up to half a billion dollars in the past eight years? Is that what the Opposition is saying?
I am also surprised by the stance taken by speakers representing the New Democratic Party. This is the Party that says it represents the "little guy". It is the "little guy" who will benefit most from the removal of quotas. Their shoes will cost less and they will find a greater selection to choose from, particularly a greater selection of lower cost footwear because the quotas had the effect of keeping out lower cost shoes.
Perhaps it is the confusion of the two opposition Parties that has led their members to be so intricate and selective in their attacks on the Government's footwear policy. Whatever the cause, their selectivity has been exquisite. I know that they have read the tribunal's report, because they keep citing it with what sounds like approval. However, what they pick out are brief passages-a sentence here, a phrase there-that, taken out of context, would make it appear that the tribunal agreed with them. It did not.
Let me cite one example of this superselectivity. The other day the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) cited a passage from the tribunal's conclusions to support his concern for the workers in the footwear industry. I certainly do not object to the Hon. Member being concerned, as I too am always concerned for workers in the industry. However, the passage that he cited was a sentence in the middle of page 57. It reads as follows:
The producers who have been identified as particularly vulnerable are smaller producers located principally in Montreal, although smaller producers in Quebec outside Montreal and perhaps also in "Ontario" may equally be at risk.

November 25, 1985
Supply
That is where he stopped. But let me read the next sentence in the report. It is as follows:
The distributions of employment by size of firm indicate that the number of workers represented by these producers is not large.
The next sentence reads:
The individual and social costs arising from loss of employment have been examined, and, in the case of Quebec, the net benefits to workers from leaving the industry are all positive.
Positive? How could that be? The tribunal offers some explanation in the Appendix section, which nobody of course has quoted. It points out that wages are low in the footwear industry, and that few workers stay at their jobs very long. Turnover is extremely high. It ranges from 56 per cent a year at the low end up to 230 per cent at the high. Two hundred and thirty per cent means that the average worker is on the job less than five months before he leaves.
In the tribunal's opinion, in other words, footwear workers taking advantage of Government programs to find new employment and upgrade their skills would be better off than they are now. That is what we intend to do for them.
The Opposition, of course, has ignored most of the tribunal's findings. It does not mention that the entire industry is still protected by 23 per cent tariffs on imported footwear, which is more than double the tariff in the United States and nearly triple that of western Europe. The Opposition cites only brief selected passages from the report, and only to try to add authority to its own curious case. I suggest that this is not proper opposition.
For the record, let me cite the tribunal's main findings. They start on page 56 of the report. The tribunal has concluded that certain sectors of the footwear industry, in the absence of special measures of protection-that is, quotas-are capable of competing successfully against imports, namely men's/boys', children's/infants', slippers/house footwear, special purpose footwear and skates. The tribunal has also concluded that women's/girls' footwear production remains vulnerable to injury from imports. The tribunal does not believe that the more vulnerable producers could expect to survive by virtue of a complex phase-out formula if they cannot compete in conditions created by a simple and straightforward process of lifting quota constraints. Accordingly, the tribunal proposes that the quotas allocations bearing upon the women's footwear sector be increased by 10 per cent per year in each of the next three years.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the Government gave the women's/girls' footwear producers, which account for roughly half of the industry's production value, more protection than the tribunal recommended. Instead of raising quotas 10 per cent a year, we are doing it more gradually, by 6 per cent the first year, 8 per cent in the second and 10 per cent in the third.
Let me stress that the Government is committed to preserving and creating jobs for Canadians. We are committed to doing this in the footwear sector and in all sectors of the economy. One of the most effective ways of creating jobs is by improving our trade performance. As I have reported to the
House, the Government is involved in a great many actions to do just that.
I suggest that the Opposition should be reminded that trade is a two-way street. We cannot expect other countries to buy our goods if we will not buy theirs. I would point out that the Opposition is carefully ignoring the fact that our trading partners are not at all happy at our decision to keep import quotas on ladies' and girls' shoes. The European Economic Community has already signalled its intention to invoke its own right to retaliate against another three years of quota by imposing restrictions on goods we export to them. I have already heard from some companies in industries that have nothing to do with footwear that they are afraid of losing their markets in Europe. If they do, they will have to lay off workers in turn.
We in Canada have been through this before. As I pointed out last week, at the time the present footwear quotas were extended to November, 1985, the European Economic Community threatened to retaliate. It threatened to raise tariffs to prohibitive levels on Canadian petrochemicals, steel products, kraft paper, furs and other products. This could have cost us $150 million a year in sales to Europe. Is the opposition saying that they are not concerned with the jobs of Canadians who work in these sectors? Do they really not care about steel workers and petrochemical workers, for example? The message is really very simple. If you provide too much protection for one industry, you will pay for it in others.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
This is a message that the Opposition does not seem to understand, but it is a fact of life. The Opposition, however, is having trouble relating to the everyday life of Canada or to the aspirations of Canadians. On this footwear issue, the Opposition has become irrelevant to Canada. It is, to put it in footwear terms, out on a limb.
The nation's press keeps up, however, and for the edification of some members of the Opposition, let me quote what some of the newspapers are reporting.
In Montreal, a La Presse editorial of November 21 read:
Ottawa has finally decided to save the Canadian footwear industry. Import quotas had created an unreal world in which the Canadian producer somehow managed to sell his production. The consumer had limited choice and high prices. The end of quotas is to the consumers' advantage and promises a new horizon for producers who can turn out quality shoes-Ottawa has taken a decision that is in the interest of the country as a whole.
What about this article from the November 22 Ottawa Citizen? it reads:
It took some nerve for the Government to drop barriers to footwear imports. The domestic industry, with visible political muscle, had been lobbying hard against the move for months. But abolishing footwear import quotas will benefit consumers-and the industry itself.
Also on November 22, Don McGillivray, the economist columnist for Southam Press, wrote:
The Tory Government has done the right thing-and a brave thing-in deciding to phase out shoe import quotas.
November 25, 1985

The Government has dared to provoke the wrath of a small, well organized and vocal section of the country to do the right thing on behalf of the consumers.
And so on, Mr. Speaker.
There has been a lot of loose talk in this House about broken promises.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: There certainly has.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Let me conclude by talking a bit about promises kept, Mr. Speaker. The Government promised to get the Canadian economy moving again, and the figures speak for themselves.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
In the 14 months we have been in office, we have created one-third of a million jobs, and unemployment has dropped from 11.6 per cent to 10.3 per cent.
When we came into office, the prime lending rate was 13 per cent. It has now dropped to 10 per cent, making it much easier and more attractive for business to invest in its future, and for Canadians to get mortgages and personal loans.
To get things moving again, we also concluded two oil agreements, the Eastern and Western Accords, replacing the destructive national energy policy of the previous Government. We did away with the Foreign Investment Review Agency, replacing it with Investment Canada. As a result, we are already beginning to get healthy doses of new foreign investment that will create jobs in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: That is not true. Investment is down, not up.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: We promised to put an end to the system of Government by fiat and introduce an era of national reconciliation, of consultation with all Canadians. We have done that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Wait until Friday.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have every respect for the fact that the Opposition cannot automatically be expected to approve everything that we do in Government. I wish the Opposition would, but I know it will not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Go down to the Maritimes to witness the First Ministers' Conference.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: I have little respect for an Opposition that attacks everything the Government does automatically and without question. It is too late to ask opposition Members to modify their stance on the footwear issue. They are already committed to it, but it may not be too late to ask them to think a bit more carefully in the future for their good as well as for the good of the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister a question. I preface it by saying that his quoting of a couple of editorialists and an economic writer simply confirms
Supply
my opinion of both those people and of the Government. It is hardly a persuasive argument to take one very traditional voice to support another traditional voice.
I want to ask the Minister to deal with one matter that I raised in my speech. No doubt it was an oversight on his part that he did not deal with it in his comments.
I pointed out that the industrial restructuring program involved in this sector had, in terms of usage of funds, used only about one-seventh of the money allocated, and that, although late in starting-and that has to be noted-the vast majority of firms now have a sort of three year modernization program under way. Since the Government was committed to the modernization of the industry and since the industry has now just started to implement these modernization programs, would it not have made much more sense for the Government to ensure that funds were spent and the industry modernized instead of, in effect, just abolishing the program now and hoping for the best?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not ignore what the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party said in his speech. I heard him, but perhaps he is right, I should have answered earlier. I am glad now I have the opportunity to do so because I do not agree with him.
With the greatest respect, I feel he is wrong and what I am saying is backed up by the finding of the tribunal itself. You have to understand, Mr. Speaker, that the tribunal found in four of the five categories that restructuring had, in fact, been done. It had been completed and the industry in those sectors was able to compete. That is why the tribunal said quotas were no longer required in those sectors and should, therefore, be removed. The move was not premature.
The tribunal said that quotas had been given their chance to operate and had operated so well and so effectively in those sectors that protection was no longer needed. The tribunal said that they should be abolished, them, and we have concurred.
The tribunal found that the womens' and girl's shoes sectors were not ready yet to compete, and that restructuring had not been completed. I agree with my hon. friend that in some areas restructuring had not been completed. I agree with my hon. friend that in some areas restructuring had not been completed and that is what the tribunal found. It said that those quotas have to be kept on for another three years, exactly what the Government is doing.
I would point out that in those areas where there may be some disruption-and I say it will be minimal because the tribunal feels that these sectors will be able to compete-the Government, together with the assistance of my hon. colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), who is in the House this morning, has put together an excellent package of support programs not only for the workers in the industry but for the companies themselves, and now, through a new initiative of my colleague's Department, for the community itself. This is very beneficial.
In some small towns the shoe industry is the only industry. The former Government did not seem to be concerned about

November 25, 1985
Supply
what could be done for those communities, but our Government has been concerned and we have implemented programs. Indeed all three, the workers, the community and the companies, will be taken care of by the package we are proposing.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the Hon. Minister. Maybe he was not in politics in May 1984 but I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that it happened by chance in your own riding.
The Prime Minister was very clear. Now, I did not know that there was a difference in the meaning of statements depending on where they are made: if you say something in a given place, it does not mean the same as when it is said some place else.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, the Minister is doing exactly what he blames us for, namely he is referring to specific sections of the Anti-dumping Tribunal's report. He takes press clippings and quotes some statements as they suit him.
But there is a constant element in the whole matter. Without quoting, because it would take too long, I remind you that on pages 52, 54, 67, 50 of the anti-dumping report, there is the unequivocal statement that thousands of jobs will be lost because of the decision you have made.
Therefore, I want to ask the Minister the following question: How many jobs will be lost because of your decision? You seem to say on one hand that there will be none. On the other hand, you say that your colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), has put together an execellent package. Therefore, will there be any jobs lost or not? If there are, how many lay-offs are anticipated? What are you going to do about the extremely painful situation in which those families who are faced with the prospect of losing their jobs in the near future find themselves?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the Opposition does not like this, but I have to keep referring back to the tribunal's decision. That inquiry took over a year, with over 72 witnesses appearing and more than 39 written briefs submitted.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: You said that already.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
That tribunal, as a result of its inquiry, said that quotas should remain on ladies' and girls' footwear. Again, Mr. Speaker, I remind my hon. friend that the production of women's and girls' shoes represents approximately 50 per cent of all shoes in Canada, with over 50 per cent of that particular production being carried on in the Province of Quebec. Given that quotas are continued on that production, there obviously is not going to be a loss of jobs in that segment of the industry.
With respect to the other sectors-and again I know you do not like to hear this-the tribunal found that no quotas were
needed. It was found that those sectors of the industry did not need production; that they could withstand the * rigours of competition. Those other sectors of the industry had restructured and updated themselves and, therefore, any disruption which would occur in those sectors, sectors in which quotas had in fact been removed, would indeed be minimal.
This Government has a concern for workers, communities and companies. Every job is precious to the person holding it, and we agree with that. Therefore, this Government wishes to put into a place a package to assist those people.
Surely to goodness you are not standing up and being critical of this Government for putting in place a package to assist people and communities and companies in the event that lay-offs do occur?
That assistance is something that this Government is proud of, and you should applaud our actions in this regard.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Minister recognize that the Government had the legal capacity to dismiss the recommendations of the Anti-dumping Tribunal? And where is the logic of his argument? I do not understand your logic. You say: We are competitive enough to face the international market. On the other hand, you say: We will face the consequences. I hardly understand your logic and I would like to hear your comments in that regard.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member raises this point about our having had the legal right not to accept the recommendation of the tribunal.
Mr. Speaker, I categorically disagree with him on that point, with great respect. The Ministry of Justice has given us a very firm opinion in that regard, and it is that, in the absence of a finding of inquiry-I repeat, in the absence of a finding of injury-under the legislation now in existence, we cannot legally impose quotas. I again remind the hon. gentleman that in four of the five categories involved, the tribunal found no injury. Therefore, in respect of those categories, we could not legally impose quotas.
I further point out to him that the legal opinion goes on to state that even in those cases where we can impose quotas, it is only for a maximum of three years.
So, not only have we done what is correct legally, we have done what is correct economically and what is in the best interests of the consumers of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing here with a very major issue as it affects the constituents of the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.There are some 400 jobs in the constituency I represent in this particular industry.
November 25, 1985

I had a conversation this morning with both shoe factories in my riding, and I am particularly concerned for the situation of the employees and management of the Alexandria Footwear factory.
Alexandria Footwear is a company owned by Rosita Shoes, and the products from that factory are most commonly known as Adidas Shoes, Adidas being, if not the best, one of the best shoes made in this country in the category of athletic footwear, and the same is true of the other shoes produced by that factory as well. Adidas shoes have gained a good reputation among all Canadian consumers.
Mr. Speaker, we are living in hard economic times. Conditions are difficult. Notwithstanding the fact that the consumers are aware that Adidas shoes are the best, they are at times faced with the hard reality, because of the economic times, of having to opt for a less expensive product. Because of the hard economic times, the consumer will often opt for the imported product, a product which is manufactured at a lower cost outside of this country.
Mr. Speaker, as of 1983 there were 172 shoe manufacturers in this country, 41 per cent of whom were located in the Province of Quebec, 56 per cent in the Province of Ontario, with the remaining 3 per cent being located in other parts of Canada.
In that year, there were in this country some 3,500 jobs in the tannery industry and some 16,000 jobs in the shoe industry.
So, close to 20,000 jobs are at stake in this industry in our country. We produce some 35 million, 36 million pair of shoes, at an estimated value of close to $1 billion.
As one can see, this industry isn't small potatoes. It is a very important industry for our country, or at least it is for those of us in the Liberal Party. Quite obviously, the Members opposite think otherwise.
Mr. Speaker, this debate today is, in large part, about truth and honesty, and one's ability to keep one's promises.
Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker-and I am sure you are aware of this-of the promises that the Tories made last year. You are aware, of course, Mr. Speaker, that I listed these promises in a little booklet called 338 Tory Promises, copies of which I will gladly give to any Hon. Member or any member of the public who writes to me. I will gladly send out a copy of this book listing the 338 Tory promises, most of which have been broken by now. Those that have not yet been broken will probably be broken in a very short time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: You'd know all about it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is listening very attentively. She was probably at the meeting in Quebec on July 26, 1984. If she was at that meeting of the Quebec caucus, she would know that a press release entitled Progressive Conservative Agenda for Government was released that day. Perhaps the Hon.
Supply
Member for Dollar (Mr. Weiner) recalls that day. This press release deals with policy area in the textile and apparel industries. That does not directly involve the footwear industry but an interesting promise was made regarding this area. Promise number one was fair trade but not free trade.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
I repeat, fair trade but not free trade. That promise was made on July 26. Today the Tories are selling off our shoe industry because it is hindering the free trade negotiations undertaken by the Tory Government.
The second promise contained within the press release deals with stability through the rigorous enforcement of our existing international rights and obligations, including if necessary the establishment of global quotas and a controlled increase in import volumes. What is so controlled about the dismantling of the system that now exists? Opening the flood gates hardly constitutes control in my book.
What have the Tories done since they came into office? They have broken just about every promise they made. Of course, I cannot say in the House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is a liar because you would not allow that, Mr. Speaker. However, I will say that the promises that were made-

speechtext: It's the threat of driving with you.

speechtext:
I note the remark of the Minister of Employment and Immigration. She has an expensive limousine at her service. She can cause the undue expense of having two cars drive to Alexandria rather than one. After all, the Prime Minister uses two jets to fly around. Perhaps, if the Minister wants a repeat performance, she could use two cars to drive to Alexandria to speak to the workers. andria should be lost. I make that challenge to any cabinet Minister.

I was saying earlier that I questioned the honesty of the promises made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign. I would like to read a few words taken from the Sherbrooke newspaper La Tribune, and I am sure that you are familiar with this quote, Mr. Speaker: "The quota policy would remain as it is, guaranteed Mr. Mulroney, who said that he was not in favour of free trade in this sector of activity."
The interview has to do with the footwear industry. This promise was made in Sherbrooke by the leader of the Progressive Conservative Party who is now Prime Minister of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read from another Canadian Press report and also from another article published in La Presse of March 25, 1985, in which the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion apparently stated that the Canadian textile, clothing and footwear industry should probably be guaranteed a share of the local market for a long period. This was last March, and I am now wondering whether a long period means six months in the mind of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. If it was deemed necessary, according to this interview with the Minister last March, to guarantee these jobs for a long period, why did he, also, break another promise made to the Canadian people?

Some Hon. Members have mentioned today that public opinion was not behind an extension of these quotas. I would like to disagree with those who have said that for the following reasons.
[ Translation]
A survey was carried out from September 16 to 20, 1985, by the Decima Research Firm of Toronto. I would like to read a few findings of this survey. The question was asked as follows: "According to some people, the Government should make use of quotas to protect the Canadian industry against foreign competition because it is important to protect jobs in Canada." People were then asked to choose one two alternatives, namely to protect jobs for Canadians or to provide greater access to less expensive products. Of the people surveyed, 66 per cent told Decima that they favoured the protection of jobs for Canadians. This means that two-thirds of Canadians do not agree with this decision made by the Conservative Party.
The following question was also asked and I quote: I would like now to ask you a few questions about the Canadian footwear industry. How important is the Canadian footwear industry to the Canadian economy and to employment in Canada. Is it very important, rather important, not very important, or not important at all? Taken together, the answers "very important" and "rather important" accounted for 84 p. 100 of all answers to that particular question.
And further on the following question was asked: In your opinion, how important is it for Canada to have its own footwear industry? Once again, 86 p. 100 of the people surveyed answered that it was very important and rather important that Canada should have its own footwear industry. speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O, 63-FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-IMPORT QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) announced last Wednesday the new footwear policy adopted by the Government. This policy represents a major step forward in the implementation of the agenda for the economic renewal of Canada which was made public a year ago. I would like to address today some of the most important elements of the new footwear import policy which have a direct bearing on the mandate of my Ministry.
As a Minister responsible for consumer interests and competition policy, I have a keen interest in trade policy, since such policy can greatly influence the state of competition in Canada and the welfare of Canadian consumers. From this perspective, I am supportive of trade liberalization measures which contribute to increase the choice of products available to Canadians and foster a healthier state of competition in the Canadian economy. On the other hand, I am generally opposed to the imposition or extension of trade barriers such as global quotas which impose heavy costs on consumers and stifle competitive forces.
I have been particularly interested in the formulation of the Government policy on footwear because it is an important question for all Canadians and because it illustrates so well the difficult choices which Canadians will have to face in the years to come. What I would like to do today is to explain to the House why I believe the Government's decision on the footwear sector import policy is the right policy. In what follows I shall focus my attention on the effects of the prior global quota regime and contrast them with those which the new Government policy are expected to have on consumers, retailers and the footwear manufacturing industry.
The consideration of the relative costs and benefits of global quotas, particularly as analysed by the report of the Canadian Import Tribunal, has been a major factor in the formulation of the policy adopted by the Government. Before I turn to these questions, I would like to point out that the previous Government, which assigned the Canadian Import Tribunal to review the industry's positiion, was clearly aware of, and concerned with, the costs associated with the adverse affects of a global quota policy when it directed the tribunal to take, and I quote:
-into account the various elements that affect the retail price of footwear in Canada, examine what impact the import quotas on footwear have had on the operations and levels of activity of importers, wholesalers and retailers of these products in Canada and on the prices paid for footwear by Canadian consumers-
November 25, 1985

To emphasize its recognition of the seriousness of these costs, the former Government went on to conclude its instructions to the tribunal in the following terms, and again I quote:
-in the event of a determination of injury or threat thereof, recommend a formula by which the special measures of protection could be phased out through a progressive liberalization process covering a period of not more than three years, by which time the Canadian industry would be required to face international competition without special measures of protection.
I believe that the previous Government was receptive in setting these terms of reference. The new policy we have adopted, which is based on the findings of the tribunal, is consistent with the analysis behind these instructions. [Translation]
As Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Mr. Speaker, I am particularly interested in the impact of quotas on Canadian consumers.
Though it is widely acknowledged that over-all quotas might protect the industry to a certain extent, they do have unfavourable effects on consumers by forcing them to pay more for goods which do not necessarily meet their needs and tastes. Shoe import quotas are not an exception to this general rule.
Evidence adduced during public hearings held by the tribunal clearly shows that quotas were responsible for higher prices for both imported and Canadian-made shoes. By restricting the supply of imported shoes, quotas make them more expensive and consumers are encouraged to buy domestically produced shoes which are relatively less costly. Stronger demand for Canadian shoes is the signal our manufacturers need to boost production and increase prices.
But quotas have a more subtle and pernicious effect than a simple across-the-board price increase: they create an artificial shortage of imported shoes, and import permit holders benefit from a shortage premium whcih amounts to an additional income. This is reflected in the difference between the price which the permit holder is able to buy his footwear on the national and world markets, and the price which he can sell them to Canadian wholesalers and retailers.
The quota system having thus given import permits a financial value, it is understandable that the holders, who have obtained these permits on the basis of their purchases over the preceding years, are unwilling to use them to purchase cheap footwear.

Mr. Speaker, last weekend Canadian National announced that it would be cutting auxilary service at Gillam, Manitoba. The auxilary is an emergen-
November 25, 1985

cy response train which goes out to deal with derailments and other emergency situations. Under CN directives an auxilary unit must be ready to leave its site within one hour. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: FUNDING OF CULTURAL INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to discuss a matter of grave importance to our cultural community. The new funding method of the Canada Council, which was adopted earlier this year, threatens the Cultural independence of our museums and galleries.

For more than twenty years, those institutions who have proven themselves have been receiving annual grants from the Canada Council. There is now a new four-part application process to obtain financial assistance. Therefore, from now on, the Canada Council will be the one to decide what exhibitions the public should see.

The effect of this new method is devastating. The museum community has found it to be more costly, and more difficult to plan its budgets and programs. For example, the Edmonton Art Gallery has already been forced to postpone many important exhibits because of Canada Council's unexplained refusal to fund them. The Gallery will incur a deficit of up to $130,000 in 1985, in large part as a direct result of Canada Council's new funding policy for major museums.
The Edmonton Art Gallery is not alone. The future remains bleak for all museums in Canada because the Council has recently stated that it will not review its new policy for two years.
1 ask the House, should an appointed body such as the Canada Council have such discretionary power over the cultural make-up of our museums and galleries? It should not be up to the Canada Council to decide what exhibition is or is not worthy of funding. I say that our local art and museum patrons should make this decision.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SUPPORT FOR SMALL AND MEDIUM-SIZED BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am prompted to rise in the House today by more good news on the economic front. A recent Gallup poll commissioned by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association proves that Canadians share the Government's conviction that the private sector is the key to economic recovery and sustained growth.
The poll results show that since 1982 the number of Canadians who believe that business is the key player in an improved economy has tripled. In addition, the number of Canadians who believe that only Government can provide the solution to economic problems has dropped by 20 per cent in the same three years.
Evidently, Canadians support our Government's policy of providing encouragement and incentives to small and mediumsized businesses. There is good reason for that support. Since September, 1984, 333,000 new jobs have been created in Canada. Unemployment is down by 1.3 per cent since the 1984 election. The response of small and medium sized businesses to the Challenge '85 program was overwhelming. Working together with provincial and federal Governments, these businesses created 100,000 jobs for Canadian students, 14,000 more than 1984's summer program.
The May 23, 1985, Budget contained many measures designed to encourage small and medium businesses. Those measures were greeted enthusiastically by the private sector then, and now Canadians across the country believe that
100,000	smaller businesses hold the key to our future prosperity.
Smaller businesses are the key to Canada's economic prosperity. Together, they and our Government will ensure our future security.

speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I want to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his statement. I would like to ask him a question on one of the problems which has led to this tragic situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, as it is my responsibility, asked me to participate in this matter, and I suggest that before people rush to the judgment that we have reached an impasse, they allow the process which is currently in train to proceed, in the hope that it will yield some results.

My question is for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I think all Members of this House were very pleased with the Minister's decision last Thursday night to begin negotiations on the comprehensive claim of the Haida people to the Queen Charlotte Islands, particularly in relation to Lyell Island and the South Moresby conflict.

Government-have agreed to come to such a meeting in Vancouver or Victoria tomorrow?

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the only thing I can do at this time which might be useful is to tell the Hon.
Oral Questions
Member that the people who are concerned with this have asked me, along with the Minister of the Environment, to continue the process toward a meeting which could begin a process of mediation.
I was in communication just prior to Question Period with members of the Haida Indian Band, and as well there was communication earlier today with the Government of British Columbia. Also, two other parties have indicated an interest in such a meeting.
I think it is far too early to arrive at any conclusions. 1 am hoping to have another day or two in order to arrive at a situation in which the opportunities may become more clear.

Mr. Speaker, the situation, as I know the Minister knows, is extremely urgent. I am wondering whether he can tell the House whether there are any additional administrative or constitutional powers, given the special relationship that this House of Commons has with the Haida people, that he might be able to make use of in this situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. David Crombie (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

subsubtopic: NEWFOUNDLAND FISHERMAN'S LOSS OF BENEFITS

However, that is one of the reasons why a case like this must be directed to the Commission of Inquiry on the Unem-

ployment Insurance Commission which may see to it that such discrepancies do not exist in the future.
In the meantime I can tell the Hon. Member that we are taking two steps. One is to ensure that the provinces concerned offer social security payments to Mr. Hawkins during the time he is in hospital. No nation is immune to the scourge of terrorism. Two innocent Canadians now join the list of victims of this international brutality. I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that this is a phenomenon that is becoming increasingly widespread, and we can no longer consider ourselves immune to this kind of occurrence. Here in Canada, we thought we were entirely immune to this kind of violence, but not long ago, the airport in Toronto was used in what increasingly appears to have been a similar act of violence, when an Air India jet crashed in the North Atlantic and another similar tragedy occurred at the airport in Tokyo, in connection with a plane coming in from Vancouver. This is not just an international problem, and I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that it is a very difficult question and one that is becoming more and more apparent, even in Canada.

However, only a few months ago, a very large number of Canadians lost their lives in the North Atlantic. The impression now seems to be that the disaster was even worse than a hijacking, since there were ammunition and explosives on board the Air India plane.
